role: Parsers of the raw result files and range functions for the facts sheet.
purpose: This module reads the raw result files of the rerun (csv files, logs, state records) and gives one rate in GB/s for every timed interval. It also holds the functions that select intervals and compute the range (lowest, highest, median) that the facts sheet reports for each kernel.

main_flow.step: The module has no main program and takes no arguments. Another script imports it. At import it derives the folder paths from its own place and imports `stat_bwx.py` and `stat_k120.py`.
`build_facts.py` reads the machine records first: `read_try6` (line 206), `read_boot_table` (line 405), and `read_log` for the logs of `go.sh` and `go2.sh` [Ref3].

Part A: for each tag of `RERUN_A`, `find` gives the folder, `read_probe` reads `probe.txt` and `read_k120` reads `threads120.csv`. Each file of the rerun gives 24 processes with 3 intervals each. The rate of an interval is the printed column `aggregate_GBps`.
Parts L and C and control I: for each tag of `RERUN_L`, `RERUN_C`, `RERUN_I`, `read_bwx` reads the one csv of the folder. It keeps the T rows of each interval.
`bwx_intervals` forms the rate of each bwx12 interval: the sum over its T rows of bytes / elapsed_s / 1e9.
`read_env` and `read_launches` read the run records of each bwx12 folder: checksum of the runner, launch time, load at launch, exit status.
`build_facts.py` copies every interval of the rerun into one record of `base_record`. `GBps` holds the rate and `rate_kind` holds `KIND_A` or `KIND_X` [Ref3].
`facts_text.py` and `facts_text4.py` pick the intervals of one kernel with `sel` and summarise them with `rng`. They compare two ranges with `overlap`, `gap` and `width_pct` [Ref4].

behavior_notes: The module reads files and writes none. Every file it opens is recorded in the list `OPENED`.

Part A rate: field 7 (`aggregate_GBps`) of each interval row, taken as printed. The binary computed it as the sum of the bytes of all threads / the longest per-thread time / 1e9 [Ref1]. The time of a thread starts at its clock read after the binary releases all threads together. It ends at its clock read after its last whole pass over the buffer. One warm-up pass of the same kernel comes before this time and is not timed [Ref1]. The `best` row and the column title row are left out. No kernel is left out: the rows of all six kernels of `bw_old` and `bw_new` are returned. For the kernels `copy` and `asmcopy` the binary counts the bytes read plus the bytes written [Ref1].

bwx rate: the sum over all T rows of one interval of bytes / elapsed_s / 1e9. Each thread is divided by its own time. No T row is left out, also not a row with the flag `late`. The 9 bwx12 csv files of the rerun (parts L and C, control I) hold no row with this flag. The value `aggregate_GBps` of the I row is kept only for a cross-check. For a read kernel `bytes` is the size of the buffer ranges that the runner gave to the kernel. For the test loop `read_1pl` this is more than the bytes that the loop loads [Ref2].

This module returns every interval of a file that it reads. The one exception is the argument `only_tags` of `read_k120`. `build_facts.py` keeps every interval of the rerun. For some bwx csv files outside the rerun it keeps only named kernels or positions (arguments `kernels` and `positions` of its function `add_bwx`) [Ref3].

The two kinds of rate are not the same formula. For the same threads the part A form (all bytes / the longest time) can never be higher than the bwx form (sum of the per-thread rates). The two are equal when all threads have the same time. Example of the size of the difference at a common stop: T72L1, `a6456.csv`, round 0, position 0, `oldread`: 462.30 GB/s from the T rows and 462.29 GB/s in the I row [Ref8]. Example of the size of the difference at the whole-pass stop of part A: the first interval row of `threads120.csv` of T72A1 has `aggregate_GBps` = 467.83 GB/s. Its column `per_thread_avg_GBps` (3.99 GB/s, rounded to 2 decimals) x 120 threads gives about 478.8 GB/s (est.) for the sum of the per-thread rates [Ref9].

This module rounds no rate. So `overlap` and `gap` compare the unrounded values of `rng`. The part A values have 2 decimals, as the binary printed them. `build_facts.py` rounds to 0.001 GB/s when it writes `facts.json` [Ref3]. `facts_text.py` rounds to 0.01 GB/s, half up, when it writes the facts sheet [Ref4].
The result for one kernel is a range, not a mean: `rng` returns the lowest value, the highest value and the median of the selected intervals. Each interval counts once.

The drop in percent of the new read kernel against the old read kernel is not formed in this module. It is also not formed from the ranges of `rng`. The function `analyse` of `facts_text.py` forms one drop per pair: (1 - new rate / old rate) x 100 [Ref4]. In part A a pair is the `bw_new` process and the `bw_old` process with the kernel `read` of the same session and round. Each of the two rates is the median of the 3 intervals of the process. For bwx12 a pair is one interval of `read` or `asmread` and the `oldread` interval of the same process and round.

The module stops the script with an error in these cases. `find`: a result folder is missing or exists twice. `read_k120`: an interval row has another kernel name than its header line. `read_bwx`: a T row does not have 13 fields. `bwx_intervals`: a kernel name does not fit the sequence of the header. `read_try6`: row 0 of `boots.txt` is not the boot of `try6.txt`, or it has another form than expected. `base_record`: the caller passes a key that the record does not have.
Most readers take values out of a matched pattern without a test. A file that lacks an expected line therefore also ends the script, with a Python error.
The `-- step` header form, the argument `only_tags` and the per-thread rows (`thread,...`) are used only for csv files of earlier runs. The csv files of the rerun of 2026-11-17 do not hold them.

words.def: the Arm reference server under test. It has 128 CPUs.
the whole-chip read test of 2026-11-17 on CRB, run after the memory speed was lowered from 8000 MT/s to 7200 MT/s.
million transfers per second, the unit of memory speed.
one DIMM. CRB has 12 slots.
the two halves of the chip. CPUs 0-63 sit on mesh 0. CPUs 64-127 sit on mesh 1.
our runs use CPUs 0-119 only: 64 threads on mesh 0 plus 56 threads on mesh 1. Each thread reads its own buffer of 256 MiB from memory.
the inner loop of the benchmark that reads memory. On this page "kernel" means this loop. The operating system kernel is always written "Linux kernel".
portable C code with 16 running sums. Each load is followed by an add. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_old and `oldread` in the runner bwx12.
NEON intrinsics (C functions that map to Arm vector instructions), loads only. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_new and `read` in bwx12.
a hand-written load-only loop. It has the same 8 "ldp q" loads per 256 B as the new read kernel. "ldp q" is the Arm instruction that loads two 16-byte vector registers.
test loops of bwx12: the asmread loop with 96 or 256 no-operation instructions per 256 B, and a loop with one load per 64 B line.
the benchmark and its two binaries of 2026-11-13. bw_old was built from the old source, bw_new from the new source.
later runner programs for the same loops. They print one row per thread. bwx12 is the runner of the 2026-11-15 investigation. bwx11 and bwx are older versions.

a process is one start of a benchmark binary. An interval is one timed measurement inside a process. bwx12 times a sequence of kernels and repeats the sequence: each repeat is a round (counted from 0), and the position is the place of a kernel in the sequence (counted from 0). In part A the round (1 or 2) is the round of the script: round 2 runs the processes in the reverse order.
one pass of go.sh through part A, part L and part C.
the 120-thread part of the test of 2026-11-13, repeated with the same two binaries.
one bwx12 process with the kernel sequence oldread, asmread, read_nop96, read_nop256, read_1pl.
one bwx12 process with the sequence oldread, read, asmread (cfwd) or asmread, read, oldread (crev).
the part L line, started from an idle machine, twice. It was added after the first numbers were seen. It is not part of the plan fixed before the run.

a named group of interval records. `build_facts.py` writes the name into the key `dataset` of each record [Ref3]. The files of the rerun give four data sets: `rerun-A`, `rerun-L`, `rerun-C` and `control-I`. Each one holds the intervals of all result folders of that part. The earlier runs have other names, for example `A-1` and `L-1`.
the arguments of one bwx12 process, as a spec file holds them. "The same line" means a process with the same arguments.
part A: the column aggregate_GBps that bandwidth.c prints. bwx runners: the sum over the threads of bytes / elapsed time. Unit GB/s.
gigabytes per second. GB = 1e9 bytes.

the row kinds of a bwx csv file: one I row per interval, one T row per thread and interval, one P row per thread before the first interval and after each interval (it holds the page state of the buffer), and one C row per thread and interval with counter values.

what a P row holds for one buffer. `kB_total` is the size of the memory area of the buffer in kB. `kB_huge` is the part of this area that lies on transparent huge pages, in kB. The four other numbers are counters of Linux for the whole system. In a run with more than one thread, bwx12 prints a comment line `# page_read` after each reading of the page state. The line holds the time that the reading took, in ms [Ref2]. In such a run a P row with `pos` = -1 holds the state before the first interval of the process. Every other P row holds the state after the interval of its `round` and `pos` [Ref2].

With the common stop, bwx12 sets one start time for all threads of an interval. It writes `late` in the last field of a T row when the thread started more than 100 microseconds after that time. In every other case it writes `-`.
the stop rule of bandwidth.c: after the minimum time (0.5 s here) each thread finishes the pass over its buffer that it is in. The threads stop at different times.

the stop rule used with bwx12 here: all threads stop at nearly the same time (after 6 s). The runner sets one deadline for all threads. Each thread stops after the 2 MiB chunk in which the deadline passes [Ref2]. In the 74 intervals of the 9 bwx12 csv files of the rerun, the end times of the 120 threads of one interval differ by less than 0.5 ms (computed from the field `t_end_s` of the T rows with `read_bwx` of this module on 2026-11-21).

total_bytes / bytes_per_thread of an interval row of part A. For the kernels read and asmread this is the number of buffer passes that all 120 threads completed in the interval. For the kernels copy and asmcopy the same division gives 2 x the number of buffer passes. The reason: the binary counts the bytes read plus the bytes written for these two kernels [Ref1].
a row that bandwidth.c prints after the interval rows of one kernel. It holds the highest aggregate_GBps of these rows [Ref1]. This module takes no value from it.
a line that go.sh or go2.sh prints with the time, the boot id, MemTotal, the load, the logins and the processes per user.

words.term: Log of go.sh, log of go2.sh
words.def: the files go-T72-20261117T221209Z.log and go2-T72-20261117T222335Z.log in R. Each file holds the standard output and the error output of one script. The command that started the script sent both outputs to the file. No script of S holds this command [Ref10].

the number of tasks that are runnable or wait for disk input and output, averaged by Linux over the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes (file /proc/loadavg). The fourth field of the file gives the tasks that are runnable now and the number of all tasks.
the column pcpu of the tool ps in the process lists of env.txt and probe.txt. It is the CPU time that a process has used, divided by the time since the process started.
a random identifier that Linux creates at each start. Equal boot ids mean the same boot.
the usable memory that Linux reports, in kB.

a short name of a run step or of a process. Three kinds occur. First, the name that go.sh or go2.sh gives to a run script (T72A1, T72L1). Second, the first field of a spec line (a6456, cfwd, crev). Third, the tag of a `-- step` line of an earlier script.
the input file of rx.sh. Each line holds a tag, the character `|` and the arguments of one runner process.
/tmp/positron-perf.RUNNING. ra.sh and rx.sh stop when this file exists.
the system log of Linux. The files read here are saved text copies with the messages of the Linux kernel.

a message that the firmware passes to Linux when hardware reports an error. Linux prints it in the kernel log with the tag "[Hardware Error]". Its severity is "corrected" (the hardware repaired it) or "recoverable" (not repaired, the system continues).
transparent huge pages of Linux. In a csv header, `thp=madvise` says that the binary asked Linux for huge pages for its buffers (call madvise with MADV_HUGEPAGE).
a value of 64 hexadecimal digits computed from the content of a file. The scripts use it to check that a binary or script is the expected file.
Coordinated Universal Time. All dates and times of day in the run files are UTC. The values `t_start_s` and `t_end_s` of a T row are not times of day. They count the seconds from the process start.
S/FACTS.md is the facts sheet: the text source for the report of the rerun. S/facts.json holds the interval records. build_facts.py writes both.
R is the results folder crb/results. S is the scratch folder of the rerun, crb/tmp/agent-scratch/w120-7200-2026-11-17.
a text file with one row per line. Commas separate the fields of a row.
the Linux policy that selects the clock frequency of a CPU.
Python terms. A tuple is a fixed list of values. `None` is the value for "no value".
a text template. A line matches when it has the form of the template. The parts in round brackets are taken out as values.

functions.name: _open
functions.what: Records the absolute path in `OPENED`, then opens the file.

functions.name: rel
functions.what: Writes a path as `R/...` or `S/...` for the facts sheet.

functions.name: sha256
functions.what: Returns the SHA-256 checksum of a file.

functions.name: folder_date
functions.what: Reads the date and time from a result folder name.

functions.name: clock
functions.what: Turns a time of day into a full date and time, with the date of the folder name.

functions.name: read_log
functions.what: Reads the state lines and the other `== ` lines of a `go.sh` or `go2.sh` log.

functions.name: read_probe
functions.what: Reads `probe.txt` of a part A folder: times, load, boot id, MemTotal, checksums.

functions.name: read_launches
functions.what: Reads `launches.txt` of `rx.sh`: one entry per launch, with its exit status.

functions.name: read_env
functions.what: Reads `env.txt` of `rx.sh`: start time, load, process list, checksum of the runner.

functions.name: read_error_records
functions.what: Lists the hardware error records of a saved journal with time, number and severity.

functions.name: step_headers
functions.what: Lists the `-- step` header lines of a csv of the earlier script `run_partA.sh`.

functions.name: read_try6
functions.what: Reads the record of 12 modules at 7200 MT/s, checks its boot id against `boots.txt` and reads `gaps.txt`.

functions.name: read_k120
functions.what: Reads a part A csv: one entry per process, with the interval rows and the printed rate `aggregate_GBps`.

functions.name: _new_section
functions.what: Returns an empty container for the rows of one bwx process.

functions.name: read_bwx
functions.what: Reads a bwx csv: header values, T rows per interval, I rows, P rows, count of C rows.

functions.name: bwx_intervals
functions.what: Forms one entry per interval: the sum of the per-thread rates, in total and per mesh, plus checks.

functions.name: find
functions.what: Returns the one result folder whose name starts with a prefix.

functions.name: read_boot_table
functions.what: Reads the boot history and the end time of the 8000 MT/s setting from the DIMM report.

functions.name: base_record
functions.what: Returns one interval record for `facts.json` with all 40 keys.

functions.name: sel
functions.what: Returns the records that match every condition.

functions.name: rng
functions.what: Returns lowest, highest and median value of a record list, with counts of intervals, processes, sessions and boots.

functions.name: overlap
functions.what: Says whether two ranges share at least one value.

functions.name: gap
functions.what: Returns the distance between the nearest ends of two ranges, with a sign.

functions.name: width_pct
functions.what: Returns the width of a range in percent of its lower end.
